html:
The great library of the Ptolemaic kings in Alexandria, founded around 285 BCE as part of the Mouseion, a research centre for scholars. It set out to collect every book in the known world and became the greatest library of antiquity.

The kings of Ptolemaic Egypt paid scholars to live and work there and bought books wherever they could. Ships in the harbour were reportedly searched for books, which were copied, with the library keeping the originals. Estimates of the number of scrolls range from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand.

Its scholars made the first library catalogue, edited the poems of Homer, and did science: Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth, and Euclid worked in the city. The library did not vanish in a single fire. It declined over centuries: scholars were expelled in a purge in 145 BCE, some books burned when Julius Caesar fought in the city in 48 BCE, and later wars wrecked the palace quarter. The story that the caliph Umar ordered it burned after the Arab conquest appeared centuries later and is not believed.
